text:
Twice a week, the party room of the Mino Club Cafe in Richmond, B.C., is converted into a classroom.

Normally, the café doubles as a children's play space and restaurant. But on Tuesdays and Saturdays, it also becomes a place to learn.

Inside, dozens of people, mostly newcomers to Canada, work hard at one thing.

"I come here want to improve my English," said Meice Xu, an immigrant from Shanghai.

It all happens under the watchful eye of Masih Sabet, who has taught over 1,000 students for free in Richmond since 2017.

"We call it [the] English Friendship Corner," said Sabet. “We help them to create friendship between themselves. And they learn that they are not alone in this.”

His lessons have been a vital service amid ongoing federal cuts to English class funding for new permanent residents and refugees.

More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

This September, Ottawa will stop funding intermediate English training altogether.

SUCCESS, a B.C.-based non-profit that helps immigrants, said it has had to close two language centres in Richmond since last year.

"We'll have to reduce the size for the upcoming year as well," said Queenie Choo, CEO of the organization.

This volunteer is teaching newcomers English for free amid federal cuts to language programs

The federal class, called Language Instruction for Newcomers to Canada, has been helping people integrate into Canadian society since 1992.

It comes in two distinct packages: Stage 1 focuses on beginner-level English to get people functioning at a basic level in Canadian society, while Stage 2 is intermediate, and often needed for people pursuing white collar work.

Both of these have been strained by funding reductions.

Federal funding for some B.C. newcomer support programs cut

'Pretty devastating': Alberta charities cut language classes after Ottawa slashes funding

But in September, it’s Stage 2 classes that will be losing all their funding from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).

From 2024 to 2027, the federal government anticipates slashing $234 million in overall settlement service provider funding.

This is money given to places like SUCCESS that help new immigrants integrate into Canada. It generally includes cash earmarked for information, employment and language services.

Protest held at Vancouver college after cuts to English language program for newcomers

The IRCC said funding is tied to the number of permanent residents coming to Canada, and that it's stopping Stage 2 English funding to prioritize basic language training.

Major immigration cuts began in 2024 when the federal government announced it would reduce the number of new permanent residents by more than 200,000.

During the first quarter of this year, Statistics Canada reported a 20 per cent drop in permanent immigrants compared with the same time last year.

Those working with newcomers say a lack of access to English classes can have consequences.

"There’s a delay in kind of the integration, delay in finding a job or delay in even the overall economic integration into the community," Choo said.

Sabet, an immigrant himself, said English classes offer an important lifeline.

"It helps them to get … out of their loneliness, helps them to get out of despair," he said.

And it can help them achieve their goals.

Xu said it makes a big difference in accomplishing simple, everyday tasks.

"I want to go to the doctor, go … shopping, even help the people," she said.

Sabet smiles when he hears this. Learning English has given him a way to be generous, and now his student wants to do the same.
